fairearn_MC_other:
It isn't just about maximal benefit. It is about encouraging mutual benefit. Let Person A have 100 units. Let Person B have 10 units. Both A and B put 100% of their units into a common account.

Allow the rate to be 3.0.

Then, the common account now 330.

One fairness is to split this 50%, which yields both individuals with more than they started with. In my world, I would prefer this option. I think it is a great evil to be greedy.

But we cannot expect all Persons A to be happy with this. Many Persons A would be unsatisfied with not receiving maximum benefit. In such a case, I am confident that many Persons A would rather keep their 100 units either in the feeling that it is unfair of them to put in their money, or purely in spite of Person B.

However, given the same scenario:

A = 100 * the multiplier of 3 = 300.
B = 10 * 3 = 30

Person A has yielded 300.
Person B has yielded 30.

Both Persons have received triple the money they started with.

Person B would of course be much happier to evenly split the total account, but Person A would be more likely to participate in general if they are allowed to keep the full 300.

This still benefits Person B, who would otherwise be completely unable to multiply their money (as no combined account would exist in the first place).

If you asked me what Person A ought to OFFER, I would say that Person A should offer to split the money, in mutual benefit. It is immoral not to.

If you ask me what the fundamental policy should be (ensuring that human nature doesn't prevent such accounts from allows Persons B from gaining more wealth), I would say that the policy should be that one gets what one puts in, and that anymore is altruism offered by Person A.
